title: 20 — Design a Metrics Monitoring and Alerting System
html:
20 — Design a Metrics Monitoring and Alerting System

The one idea: metrics are time series — (name, labels, timestamp, value) — written constantly and queried mostly over the last few hours. Use a purpose-built time-series store, buffer ingestion through a queue, downsample old data, and evaluate alert rules on a schedule against the store, not in the ingestion path.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Internal system for a large company: 100M DAU, 1,000 server pools × 100 machines × 100 metrics ≈ 10M metrics.
  • Metrics: CPU, memory, disk, request count, error rates, queue depth…
  • Retention: raw 7 days, 1-minute resolution for 30 days, 1-hour resolution for 1 year.
  • Alerts via email, phone, PagerDuty, webhooks.
  • Out of scope: logs (ELK), distributed tracing.

Qualities: scalable, low query latency for dashboards and alerts, reliable (don't miss critical alerts), flexible (new tech plugs in).

Step 2 — High-level design

Data model

metric_name  cpu.load
labels       host=i631, env=prod, region=us-west
timestamp    1613707265
value        0.29

A series is identified by name + labels. Queries aggregate across labels (avg CPU for region=us-west).

Access pattern

  • Writes: constant, heavy (millions of points per second).
  • Reads: spiky (dashboards, alert evaluation), mostly recent data.

Storage: a general-purpose RDBMS or even Cassandra struggles with this at scale — use a time-series database (Prometheus, InfluxDB, M3, Timescale) with compression (delta-of-delta timestamps, XOR floats à la Gorilla) and label indexes.

---
title: Metrics monitoring — high-level architecture
---
flowchart LR
    Src["Metrics sources<br/>(servers, apps, DBs)"] --> Col["Metrics collectors"]
    Col --> K["Kafka"]
    K --> Con["Consumers<br/>(Flink/Storm)"]
    Con --> TSDB[("Time-series DB")]
    TSDB --> QS["Query service"]
    QS --> Cache[("Query cache")]
    QS --> Viz["Visualisation<br/>(Grafana)"]
    QS --> AS["Alerting system"]
    AS --> Ch["Email / SMS / PagerDuty / webhook"]

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Collection: pull vs push

Pull (Prometheus) Push (CloudWatch, OTLP push)
How Collector scrapes /metrics endpoints Agents send to collector
Discovery Needs service discovery (etcd, K8s API) Sources know the collector's address
Health detection Failed scrape = target down ✅ Missing data could be down or network
Short-lived jobs Missed ✅ Push works
Firewalls / multi-DC Collector needs reach to every target Easier — outbound only

Both are fine; many systems use both. Scale collectors with consistent hashing over targets so each is scraped once.

3.2 Scaling ingestion

Put Kafka between collectors and the TSDB: decouples, buffers during TSDB outages, and lets you partition by metric name so aggregation can happen per partition.

3.3 Where to aggregate

Where Pro Con
Collection agent Less data sent Only simple aggregation
Ingestion pipeline (Flink) Much less stored Lose raw precision; late events tricky
Query time Raw data kept, full flexibility Slower queries

3.4 Storage optimisation

  • Encoding/compression: delta-of-delta timestamps, XOR-compressed values → ~1.4 bytes/point (Gorilla).
  • Downsampling: raw → 1-min → 1-hour rollups as data ages.
  • Cold storage for old, rarely read data.

3.5 Alerting

---
title: Alerting pipeline
---
flowchart LR
    Rules[("Rule configs<br/>YAML")] --> AM["Alert manager"]
    AM -->|"evaluate every N s"| QS["Query service"]
    AM --> AStore[("Alert store<br/>state: inactive/pending/firing/resolved")]
    AM --> AK["Kafka"] --> AC["Alert consumers"] --> Ch["Channels"]
  • Rules: avg(cpu) by (host) > 0.9 for 5m.
  • Dedupe, merge, and group alerts (one incident, not 1,000 pages).
  • Access control; retry until delivered (at-least-once).

3.6 Visualisation

Build vs buy → Grafana almost always.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Pull vs push, Kafka buffering, TSDB choice with compression and downsampling, alerting off the ingest path, and buy-don't-build for visualisation (and often for the whole stack).

.NET / Azure mapping

  • .NET metrics API: System.Diagnostics.Metrics (Meter, Counter<T>, Histogram<T>) — the native instrument; exported via OpenTelemetry (AddOpenTelemetry().WithMetrics(...)) to Prometheus (pull, /metrics) or OTLP (push).
  • Azure Monitor Metrics + Application Insights — the managed stack; alert rules (static or dynamic thresholds), action groups for email/SMS/webhook/Logic Apps.
  • Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus + Azure Managed Grafana — the Prometheus/Grafana model without running them.
  • Azure Data Explorer (Kusto) — time-series analytics at scale; KQL make-series, series_decompose_anomalies().
  • dotnet-counters for live inspection of a process's metrics.

Review checklist

  • Data model: name + labels + time + value.
  • Write-heavy access pattern → TSDB, not an RDBMS.
  • Pull vs push trade-offs.
  • Kafka buffer between collection and storage.
  • Compression + downsampling + retention tiers.
  • Alert evaluation, dedupe/grouping, delivery guarantees.
